meta.titre: Domestic electricity: power, energy bills and safe wiring
meta.sous_theme: Power, energy in kWh, cost, fuses and house wiring

sections.contenu_markdown: At the end of the month the ENEO bill arrives, and families in Yaounde want to know why it is so high. The answer is in the power of the appliances, how long they are used, and the price of one kilowatt-hour. Behind the walls, the wires, fuses and earth connection decide whether the house is safe. The GCE examiners ask you to calculate current, energy and cost, choose a fuse, and explain the role of the earth wire and of the ring circuit.

items: Power is the rate of transferring energy: $P = E/t$, measured in watts.
Electrical power is given by $P = IV$.
Mains electricity in Cameroon is an alternating supply of about $220\,\mathrm{V}$ at $50\,\mathrm{Hz}$.

sections.titre: Electrical power, energy cost and house wiring
sections.contenu_markdown:
**Power and energy.** The power of an appliance in watts is $P = IV$, so the current in a working appliance is

$$I = \frac{P}{V}$$

The energy transferred is $E = Pt$. The joule is a very small unit for the electricity bill, so the **kilowatt-hour** (kWh) is used: it is the energy used by a $1\,\mathrm{kW}$ appliance in 1 hour, and $1\,\mathrm{kWh} = 3.6\times10^{6}\,\mathrm{J}$.

$$\text{energy (kWh)} = \text{power (kW)} \times \text{time (h)} \qquad \text{cost} = \text{energy (kWh)} \times \text{price per kWh}$$

**The three wires.** A socket has a live wire (the supply at high potential), a neutral wire (the return path) and an earth wire (a safety connection to the ground). The switch and the fuse are always placed in the **live** wire, so that when the switch is off or the fuse has blown, the appliance is not connected to the high potential.

**The fuse** is a thin wire that melts and breaks the circuit if the current is larger than its rating. Choose the smallest available rating that is just above the normal current of the appliance (standard values are $3\,\mathrm{A}$, $5\,\mathrm{A}$ and $13\,\mathrm{A}$). **The earth wire** connects the metal case of an appliance to the ground. If the live wire touches the case, a large current flows through the earth wire and blows the fuse, so the case never stays at a dangerous potential and the user is protected.

variantes.quand_utiliser: when asked to describe house circuits or to compare a ring circuit with a linear (radial) one
variantes.contenu_markdown: Appliances in a house are connected in parallel across the supply, so each one gets the full $220\,\mathrm{V}$ and can be switched on and off independently. In a **ring circuit**, a cable starts at the fuse box, goes round the house past all the sockets, and returns to the fuse box, so the current to a socket arrives by two paths. Advantages over a linear circuit: thinner cable can be used because the current is shared by the two paths; each socket still works if the cable breaks at one point; and less wiring is needed. Each plug carries its own fuse.

variantes.nom: Circuit breakers and other safety devices
variantes.quand_utiliser: when asked for another way of protecting a circuit
variantes.contenu_markdown: A circuit breaker is an electromagnetic switch that opens automatically when the current becomes too large; unlike a fuse it can be reset and used again. Other precautions: never touch switches with wet hands, use insulated cables, do not overload a socket with many appliances, and replace a blown fuse only by one of the same rating.

variantes.quand_utiliser: when the question gives the power, hours of use and price per unit
variantes.contenu_markdown: Method: (1) convert the power to kW; (2) multiply by the time in hours to get kWh; (3) multiply by the price per kWh. For several appliances, find the energy of each and add. Use the total number of days when the question asks for a month.

sections.enonce_markdown: An electric iron is rated $880\,\mathrm{W}$, $220\,\mathrm{V}$. Fuses of ratings $3\,\mathrm{A}$, $5\,\mathrm{A}$ and $13\,\mathrm{A}$ are available. (a) Calculate the normal current in the iron and choose the correct fuse. (b) The iron is used for $2.5$ hours every day. Calculate the energy used in 30 days in kWh, and its cost at an assumed price of 75 FCFA per kWh.

etapes.justification: The current in an appliance is $I = P/V$.
A fuse must be rated just above the normal current: $3\,\mathrm{A}$ would blow at once, and $13\,\mathrm{A}$ would allow dangerous overloads.
The kilowatt-hour requires power in kW.

etapes.action: Calculate the energy used in 30 days.
etapes.justification: Energy $=$ power $\times$ time, with time in hours.

sections.conclusion_markdown: The iron carries $4.0\,\mathrm{A}$, so a $5\,\mathrm{A}$ fuse is needed. Used for 30 days, it consumes $66\,\mathrm{kWh}$, which costs **4950 FCFA** at the assumed tariff.

items.erreur_markdown: The fuse should be placed in the neutral wire.
items.pourquoi_faux: If the fuse is in the neutral wire and it blows, the appliance is still connected to the live wire, so the case or the element can still be at a dangerous potential.
items.correction_markdown: Put the fuse and the switch in the live wire.

items.erreur_markdown: A $13\,\mathrm{A}$ fuse is suitable for a $60\,\mathrm{W}$ lamp because it is the largest, so it never blows.
items.pourquoi_faux: The current in the lamp is under $0.3\,\mathrm{A}$. A $13\,\mathrm{A}$ fuse would let a large fault current flow before it melted, so the wire could overheat and start a fire.
items.correction_markdown: Choose the rating just above the normal current: here a $3\,\mathrm{A}$ fuse.

items.erreur_markdown: A kilowatt-hour is a unit of power.
items.pourquoi_faux: A kWh is power multiplied by time, so it is a unit of energy ($3.6\times10^{6}\,\mathrm{J}$). The kilowatt is the unit of power.
items.correction_markdown: kW is power; kWh is energy; the bill is for energy.

items.erreur_markdown: Calculating the cost with the power in watts, for example $880 \times 2.5 \times 75$.
items.pourquoi_faux: The price is per kilowatt-hour, so the power must be in kW. Using watts makes the cost 1000 times too large.

items.erreur_markdown: The earth wire carries the normal working current of the appliance.
items.pourquoi_faux: The earth wire is only a safety connection. It carries a current only when a fault makes the case live. The working current flows in the live and neutral wires.
items.correction_markdown: The earth wire protects the user by letting the fault current flow to the ground and blow the fuse.

items.enonce_markdown: A $100\,\mathrm{W}$ lamp is switched on for $8$ hours. Calculate the energy used in kWh and the cost at 75 FCFA per kWh.
items.solution_markdown:
Power $= 100\,\mathrm{W} = 0.100\,\mathrm{kW}$.

Energy $= 0.100 \times 8$, so **$E = 0.8\,\mathrm{kWh}$**.

Cost $= 0.8 \times 75$, so **cost $= 60$ FCFA**.

items.enonce_markdown: An electric kettle is rated $2200\,\mathrm{W}$, $220\,\mathrm{V}$. (a) Calculate the current in the kettle. (b) Which of the fuses $3\,\mathrm{A}$, $5\,\mathrm{A}$ and $13\,\mathrm{A}$ should be used? (c) The kettle is used for $6$ minutes. Calculate the energy used in kWh and its cost at 75 FCFA per kWh.
items.solution_markdown:
(a) $I = \dfrac{P}{V} = \dfrac{2200}{220}$, so **$I = 10\,\mathrm{A}$**.

(b) The fuse must be just above $10\,\mathrm{A}$: **the $13\,\mathrm{A}$ fuse**. The $3\,\mathrm{A}$ and $5\,\mathrm{A}$ fuses would melt immediately.

(c) $2200\,\mathrm{W} = 2.2\,\mathrm{kW}$ and $6\,\text{min} = 0.1\,\mathrm{h}$. $E = 2.2 \times 0.1$, so **$E = 0.22\,\mathrm{kWh}$**. Cost $= 0.22 \times 75$, so **cost $= 16.5$ FCFA**.

items.enonce_markdown: A small household uses, each day, three lamps of $60\,\mathrm{W}$ for $5$ hours, a fridge of $120\,\mathrm{W}$ running for $10$ hours and a television of $80\,\mathrm{W}$ for $6$ hours. (a) Calculate the energy used by each appliance group in one day, in kWh. (b) Calculate the total cost for 30 days at 75 FCFA per kWh. (c) How much of this cost is due to the television?
items.solution_markdown:
(a) Lamps: $3 \times 0.060 \times 5 = 0.90\,\mathrm{kWh}$. Fridge: $0.120 \times 10 = 1.20\,\mathrm{kWh}$. Television: $0.080 \times 6 = 0.48\,\mathrm{kWh}$.

(b) Total per day $= 0.90 + 1.20 + 0.48 = 2.58\,\mathrm{kWh}$. For 30 days: $2.58 \times 30 = 77.4\,\mathrm{kWh}$. Cost $= 77.4 \times 75$, so **cost $= 5805$ FCFA**.

(c) Television per day $= 0.48 \times 75 = 36$ FCFA, so over 30 days $36 \times 30$, which is **1080 FCFA**.

items_markdown: $P = IV$, so $I = P/V$; energy $E = Pt$. The bill is for energy in kWh: $\text{kWh} = \text{kW} \times \text{h}$ and $\text{cost} = \text{kWh} \times \text{price}$.
The **fuse** and the **switch** go in the **live** wire; choose a fuse rating just above the normal current.
The **earth wire** joins the metal case to the ground; if a fault makes the case live, a large current flows to earth and blows the fuse.
Appliances are wired in **parallel** so each gets the full voltage and works independently; a **ring circuit** shares the current between two paths so thinner cable can be used.
A **circuit breaker** is a resettable electromagnetic switch that cuts the supply when the current is too high.
